source.title: The Impact of Reinitialization on Generalization in Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Ibrahim M. Alabdulmohsin; Hartmut Maennel; Daniel Keysers

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some mathematical symbols and table formatting are flattened, but the reported values used below can be assigned from the surrounding text and table headings.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own experiments on how reinitialization affects test accuracy and generalization in CNNs, a related training-procedure condition. It does not test the specific conditions or measurements in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper compares reinitialization methods with a baseline and reports test accuracy, but none of the claim versions names reinitialization. It cites prior work on random-label memorization and sharpness; those cited results are not rows here.
record.test_reason: Tables 2 and 7 directly test V6: they report test accuracy with augmentation held fixed and dropout changed from 0 to 0.25, with other hyperparameters unchanged. The record overlooks this comparison. Reinitialization results and unscaled Gaussian perturbation sensitivity do not themselves test V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that bottom-up layerwise reinitialization improves CNN generalization particularly on small datasets, associate this with increased margins and flatter minima, and report no apparent large-dataset benefit. These associations are proposed explanations rather than established causal mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and compares reinitialization procedures, including layerwise reinitialization with rescaling and normalization, against standard baseline training; it does not reproduce the original methods represented by V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that reinitialization performance varies with dataset size and architecture; it also examines augmentation, dropout, initializer, learning rate, momentum, and weight decay settings. It notes that for large training sets with ResNet50, most methods perform as well as baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: At α=0.5, baseline and LW test accuracies are 20.3±0.6% and 25.2±0.8%; all methods attain perfect training accuracy. At α=1 and α=2, LW also improves test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layerwise reinitialization can improve generalization on this synthetic signal-plus-noise task despite perfect training accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding reinitialization to rescaling and normalization increases VGG16 accuracy from approximately 66% to 75% on CIFAR10 and 34% to 42% on CIFAR100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reinitialization contributes accuracy gains beyond rescaling and normalization in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Freezing early layers can cause training collapse; omitting normalization can reduce test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The success of layerwise reinitialization depends on fine-tuning and normalization choices.

fits_no_version.finding: LW solutions are reported to be less sensitive than baseline solutions to isotropic Gaussian parameter perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layerwise reinitialization can improve robustness to unscaled parameter perturbations.

record.problems: The paper notes that fixed hyperparameters are suboptimal for some architecture and dataset combinations. Some appendix results are described approximately in text or shown in figures; no uncertainty is given for the cited VGG16 ablation accuracies. The excerpt does not provide the numeric values from Figure 5.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports extensive per-dataset, per-architecture accuracy tables for baseline and five reinitialization methods (Tables 2, 6, and 7), plus broad hyperparameter sweeps. Those results are not separately transcribed because the study tests none of V1–V8 and the table matrices contain many distinct subject-condition rows; the selected rows capture the synthetic example, a stated ablation with explicit comparisons, and the perturbation measurement.

untested.parts: No matched natural-label and fixed random-label training experiment.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.

No systematic dropout-rate or training-set-size sweep establishing excessive-dropout underfitting or the very-small-data exception; no joint removal of dropout and weight decay. Tables 2 and 7 test dropout 0 versus 0.25 with augmentation.
No magnitude-scaled perturbation measure, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison of predictive rankings against norm and margin measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence.

missing.what: Matched dropout comparisons linking V6 to test accuracy: transcribe corresponding cells from Tables 2 and 7, holding dataset, architecture, augmentation, and training method fixed. Although rows_left_out declares the benchmark matrices omitted, it incorrectly treats them as irrelevant to every version. The V6 verdicts above use their baseline-column comparisons directly.

record.verdict_notes: No supplied row directly records the dropout intervention, so V6 verdicts rely on the supplied table text pending row additions. Reported table differences lack uncertainty estimates; small changes should not be described as statistically established dropout effects. No external sources or files were accessed.

versions.untested_parts: No natural-label versus random-label comparison of the same architecture and recipe.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No fully connected image classifier comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
Dropout appears as an experiment setting, but the study does not report a direct dropout-versus-no-dropout effect as a result.
The paper compares standard Gaussian perturbation sensitivity for LW and baseline; it does not test magnitude-aware sharpness or rank the generalization gaps among similarly low-loss networks.

relationships.condition: Augmented baseline CNNs in settings with substantial accuracy gains from dropout 0.25
relationships.reason: Missing rows, Tables 2 and 7: VGG16 accuracy rises from 22.0% to 25.3% on Oxford-IIIT, 11.7% to 14.3% on Cars196, and 53.2% to 56.7% on CIFAR100; ResNet50 on Cassava rises from 46.5% to 74.2%. These directly demonstrate beneficial dropout regimes.
relationships.display_finding: Dropout reportedly improved test accuracy in these settings, but the comparisons remain unverified and lack uncertainty estimates.
